title: The Midwife Who Invented Cesarean Survival
event_summary: In 1879, British missionary-doctor Robert William Felkin witnessed a Banyoro healer in the kingdom of Bunyoro perform a successful cesarean section on a young woman, using banana wine as both antiseptic and anesthetic, cauterizing the wound with heated iron, and closing the incision with acacia thorns and a paste of herbs. The mother and child both survived. Felkin documented the procedure in detail in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1884, noting that the technique appeared routine and well-practiced, suggesting a long surgical tradition predating European antiseptic methods by generations.
why_forgotten: Colonial medical establishments were deeply invested in narratives of European scientific superiority and dismissed African surgical knowledge as anecdotal or primitive. Felkin's account, though published in a respected journal, was treated as a curiosity rather than evidence of a sophisticated indigenous medical tradition. The Scramble for Africa soon dismantled Bunyoro's political structures, and the kingdom's medical practitioners were never systematically studied or credited.
why_it_matters: This documented procedure predated the widespread survival of cesarean patients in European hospitals, where maternal mortality from the operation remained catastrophically high well into the 1880s. It demonstrates that antiseptic and anesthetic surgical principles were independently developed in East Africa, challenging the Eurocentric timeline of modern surgery. Today, as global health organizations work to reduce maternal mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, this history reframes the region not as a passive recipient of Western medicine but as a place with deep, sophisticated surgical heritage that was actively erased.
